title: The small village
hookLine: a small country where people hear the neighbor's dogs and roosters but are content at home (Tao Te Ching 80)

lines: A COUNTRY THE SIZE OF A VILLAGE.
cards: A rooster, somewhere over the fence, before it's light. A dog two yards down answers it. A screen door.
Somebody's radio. You could map the whole block by ear without ever seeing it. And still, the usual plan for the day is to get off that street: into the car, onto the highway, into the next thing.
Chapter eighty of the Tao Te Ching stays on the street. It paints a whole country the size of a village, and it lets you hear the neighbors' animals through the walls.

teach.b: First, the size. Let the country be small, the chapter says, with few people. Give them tools that could do the work of many hands, and they leave them unused.
Second, what they don't do. They take death seriously, so they don't wander far.

teach.h: BOATS, BUT NO NEED TO RIDE.
teach.b: They have boats and carriages, but no reason to ride in them. Armor and weapons, but no occasion to lay them out. They even go back to knotting cords to keep their records.
They find their food sweet, their clothes fine, their homes restful, their customs a pleasure. Nothing on that list is new or rare. It's their own plate, their own coat, their own roof.

teach.h: THEY HEAR THE DOGS NEXT DOOR.
teach.b: The next country is so close they can see it, and hear its roosters crow and its dogs bark. And yet the people grow old and die without ever going back and forth. Readers take this differently.
Some hear a dream of a simpler age, a ruler's picture of a quiet state.
Some hear a picture of a heart so at home that the far side of the fence doesn't pull at it. Nobody in the chapter is unfriendly. There's no wall, no quarrel, no fear of the neighbors.
The barking is just a sound in the evening. Brought down to a weeknight, it looks like eating dinner and tasting it.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eighty in more than one way: some read it as a picture of a simple, peaceful state, others as a picture of a contented life that doesn't need to chase what's beyond the fence.

o: a tiny, content land where nobody needs to leave home
a hidden village where sages escape from the world
a farming town that has to trade with its neighbors

games.q: inside the small village: tap the pairs.
p: no reason to ride in them
no occasion to lay them out
close enough to hear its dogs

s: in chapter eighty, the villagers fear and avoid their neighbors
there's no quarrel or wall in the chapter. they hear the dogs next door and are simply content at home.
the people in the chapter have boats and carriages
they have them, but no reason to ride in them.
chapter eighty asks for a large country with many people
it opens: let the country be small, with few people.

games.q: you live in the small village. you can hear the roosters in the next country every morning. what does the chapter say the people do?
o: take a boat over to see it.
build a wall so they can't hear it.
grow old at home without going back and forth.
games.why: they grow old and die without visiting. not out of fear: their food is sweet and their homes restful, so the far side doesn't pull at them.

practice: Listen outward, past the room, to whatever reaches you from where you live: a car, a bird, a neighbor's door, the fridge humming, the wind. Don't go toward the sounds; let them come to you.
Then bring to mind one ordinary thing at home, a cup you like, a chair, a window, and let it be enough for a moment.

wordCard.voice: The small village. Chapter eighty: a small country where people find their food sweet and their homes restful, and hear the neighbors' dogs without needing to go. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: a small country, few people, the opening words of chapter eighty.

carryVoice: Your line: content at home. Your own plate and your own roof were on the chapter's list, too. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 80 (a small state with few people; boats and carriages unused, armor not displayed; knotted cords; sweet food, fine clothes, restful homes, pleasant customs; neighbors' cocks and dogs heard, yet the people grow old and die without going back and forth)
